_work.title: Islamic Talismanic Objects: Shirts, Scrolls, Bowls and Amulets
_work.blurb: Physical talismans from the Islamic world: Ottoman and Safavid-era shirts inscribed top-to-bottom with Quranic verses, divine names, magic squares (wafq), and zodiacal symbols; prayer scrolls; brass talismanic bowls with serpent-and-zodiac ornament. These wearable and portable objects embody the practical side of the learned Islamic occult tradition documented in texts like the Picatrix, al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif, and the Solomonic seal literature.

entries.title: Ottoman Talismanic Shirt (exterior), MET — 15th–16th c.
entries.summary: Front view of an Ottoman talismanic shirt (Metropolitan Museum of Art) covered in dense Quranic inscriptions, divine names, and geometric magic squares (wafq) in several ink colours. Worn in battle or during illness, such shirts were believed to protect through the power of the sacred text and the numerical harmonies of the wafq. The MET holds several examples from the 15th–16th century.

entries.title: Ottoman Talismanic Shirt (interior), MET — 15th–16th c.
entries.summary: Interior view of the same MET Ottoman talismanic shirt, showing the dense application of sacred script and wafq grids to every surface. The practice of inscribing garments with protective formulae draws on the Solomonic and al-Buni traditions of letter-magic (ilm al-huruf) and the science of the names of God.

entries.title: Ottoman Talismanic Shirt (MET ISL107) — 15th–16th c.
entries.summary: A second Ottoman talismanic shirt at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (ISL107), its surface covered with multicolour calligraphic panels and geometric wafq squares. Such objects were commissioned for rulers and warriors; several were reportedly worn by Suleyman the Magnificent. They represent the material instantiation of learned Islamic occult science.

entries.title: Ottoman Talismanic Shirt (front), MET DT322190
entries.summary: Front view of an Ottoman talismanic shirt at the Metropolitan Museum. The chest panel is organised into a grid of named wafq squares corresponding to the planets, divine attributes, and prophets. Each cell is a self-contained protective unit; the whole garment is a cosmological diagram made wearable.

entries.title: Khalili Collection Talismanic Shirt — Ottoman, 16th c.
entries.summary: A 16th-century Ottoman talismanic shirt from the Khalili Collection. Distinguished from the MET examples by its Hajj pilgrimage iconography in addition to the wafq squares and Quranic verses. Worn as protection during the pilgrimage to Mecca, it integrates the talismanic and the devotional.

entries.title: Polygonal Talisman (Khalili Collection, tls 0051)
entries.summary: A double-sided polygonal talisman from the Khalili Collection of Islamic Art. The front face bears divine names and Quranic verses in a structured geometric layout; the reverse carries corresponding numerical wafq squares. Khalili Islamic Art tls 0051.

entries.title: Islamic Talisman (Khalili Collection, tls 0053)
entries.summary: A metalwork talisman from the Khalili Collection of Islamic Art (tls 0053). Inscribed with Quranic verses, divine attributes, and protective formulae in a format typical of the learned Islamic occult tradition as documented in al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif.

entries.title: Islamic Talisman (Khalili Collection, tls 1966)
entries.summary: A metalwork talisman from the Khalili Collection of Islamic Art (tls 1966), with inscribed protective formulae and geometric division typical of the wafq tradition. The Khalili Collection holds one of the largest public collections of Islamic talismanic objects.

entries.title: Talismanic Prayer Scroll (ACM-03625)
entries.summary: A talismanic prayer scroll from an Islamic collection, written on a long strip of paper or vellum and folded to be worn on the body or hung in the home. Such scrolls combine Quranic verses, divine names, angelic names, and magic squares (wafq) in a continuous talismanic text. The form is closely related to the European armatura and phylactery.

entries.title: Talismanic Prayer Scroll (ACM-03629)
entries.summary: A second talismanic prayer scroll from the Aga Khan Museum collection. The alternating bands of script and geometric patterning are characteristic of the Islamic talismanic scroll tradition. Worn on the body or rolled inside a metal case, these objects represent the portable dimension of learned Islamic magic.

entries.title: Talismanic Brass Bowl with Serpent and Zodiac
entries.summary: A talismanic brass bowl decorated with a knotted serpent and zodiacal medallions. Such bowls were used for healing: water poured into the bowl was believed to absorb the protective power of the inscriptions and could be drunk by the patient. The serpent motif recalls the Solomonic seal tradition and the healing properties attributed to the planet Mercury.

entries.title: Persian Manuscript on Talismans
entries.summary: A page from a Persian manuscript on talismanic science, showing diagrams of protective seals and inscribed figures. Persian talismanic literature drew on both the Arabic learned tradition (al-Buni, Picatrix) and indigenous Iranian magical practices, producing a distinctive synthesis of Quranic letter-magic, astrological imagery, and Solomonic seal forms.

entries.title: "Caesar Makes a Talisman", Shahnama Folio (MET, CC0)
entries.commons_file: File:"Caesar Makes a Talisman", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) MET DP223864.jpg
entries.summary: A folio from a 14th-century Ilkhanid Shahnama (Book of Kings) at the Metropolitan Museum of Art depicting Caesar crafting a talisman. In Firdausi's epic, Caesar represents the learned Greco-Roman sage; his talisman-making scene illustrates the intersection of Persian heroic narrative and the inherited tradition of learned image-magic. Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0.

entries.title: Islamic Talisman, Louvre MAO904 — 18th–19th c.
entries.summary: A copper-alloy Islamic talisman in the Louvre collection (MAO904). The engraved surface bears divine names, geometric wafq squares, and protective formulas in Arabic script. This type of object represents the intersection of metalsmithing, calligraphy, and learned occult science in the Islamic world.

entries.title: Shi’i Stamped Amulet with Magic Squares and Zulfikar
entries.summary: A 19th-century Shi'i amulet showing magic squares (wafq), Quranic verses, and the image of Zulfikar (Ali's sword). Shi'i talismanic practice developed its own iconographic vocabulary combining the standard Islamic wafq tradition with devotion to the Imams, depicted here through Zulfikar, the emblem of Ali ibn Abi Talib.

entries.title: Al-Buni Magic Manuscript, Khalili mss 0300 (fol. 108b–109a)
entries.summary: Folios 108b–109a from Khalili Collection Islamic Art MS 0300, an al-Buni-related magic manuscript. Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. 1225) wrote the encyclopaedic Shams al-Ma'arif (Sun of Gnoses), the most influential Arabic compendium of letter-magic, divine names, magic squares, and talismanic science. The Khalili manuscript preserves diagrams of wafq grids and named squares.

entries.title: Francis Barrett’s Magic Squares Plate from *The Magus* (1801)
entries.summary: The first plate of magic squares (planetary kamea) from Francis Barrett's *The Magus* (London, 1801), reproducing Agrippa's planetary magic-square system: Saturn 3x3, Jupiter 4x4, Mars 5x5, Sol 6x6, Venus 7x7, Mercury 8x8, Luna 9x9. Barrett's *Magus* was a key conduit for Cornelius Agrippa's Renaissance occult philosophy into the 19th-century occult revival.

entries.title: Buduh Magic Square (al-Qazwini, 13th c.)
entries.summary: The Buduh magic square from al-Qazwini's *Aja'ib al-Makhluqat* (Wonders of Creation, c. 1280). Buduh (b-d-w-h) is a four-letter divine name whose letters, assigned numerical values, yield the classic 3x3 magic square. This is the foundational wafq of the Islamic talismanic tradition, discussed by al-Buni and applied to amulets, garments, and magical operations across the Islamic world.
